questions.stem: Under MQSA, what must a facility obtain before it can be issued an FDA certificate?

choices.text: Accreditation by an FDA-approved accreditation body
choices.rationale: Correct. FDA issues a certificate after the facility meets the quality standards and is accredited by an approved accreditation body (or other FDA-designated entity).

choices.text: ARRT certification and registration for every technologist
choices.rationale: MQSA requires State licensure or general certification plus mammography training; it does not make ARRT credentials the basis for facility certification.

choices.text: A passing result on the facility's first annual inspection
choices.rationale: Inspections check certified facilities. The certificate is based on accreditation, not on a prior inspection.

choices.text: A State radiation-control license for each unit
choices.rationale: State rules may apply separately, but the MQSA certificate depends on accreditation and meeting § 900.12.

questions.explanation: Accreditation comes first: an approved accreditation body reviews the facility, and FDA (or a State certification agency) issues the certificate.

variants.simpler: No accreditation, no certificate. The accreditation body's review is the basis for FDA's approval.
variants.example: A facility whose accreditation is denied cannot obtain an FDA certificate, even with excellent staff.

questions.stem: A new facility receives a provisional MQSA certificate. Which statement about it is accurate?

choices.text: It lasts 12 months and can be renewed once.
choices.rationale: The provisional certificate lasts up to 6 months and cannot be renewed.

choices.text: It lasts up to 6 months; it cannot be renewed, but one 90-day extension may be requested.
choices.rationale: Correct. This matches § 900.11(b)(2)–(3).

choices.text: It allows screening only; diagnostic exams wait for full certification.
choices.rationale: The regulation describes the provisional certificate as enabling the facility to perform mammography; it doesn't split screening from diagnostic.

choices.text: It lasts 3 years, matching the clinical image review cycle.
choices.rationale: Three years is the accreditation body's clinical image review frequency, not the provisional certificate's length.

questions.explanation: The provisional certificate exists so the facility can perform exams and collect the clinical images needed for accreditation. Up to 6 months, no renewal, one possible 90-day extension.

variants.simpler: Six months to finish accreditation, plus at most one 90-day extension.
variants.example: A rural facility that would leave its county without mammography could document that impact when asking for the 90-day extension.

questions.stem: Which mammography facility is NOT subject to the MQSA facility quality standards in 21 CFR 900 Subpart B?

choices.rationale: Hospital outpatient departments are included in the definition of facility.
Mobile units are explicitly included in the definition of facility.

choices.text: A Department of Veterans Affairs facility
choices.rationale: Correct. Subpart B excludes Department of Veterans Affairs facilities.
Offices of a physician that conduct mammography are included.

questions.explanation: Subpart B applies to all facilities under U.S. regulatory jurisdiction providing mammography, except the Department of Veterans Affairs.

variants.simpler: Almost everyone is covered. The named exception is the VA.
variants.example: A mobile coach that serves workplaces is still a facility under MQSA.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the eight attributes an accreditation body uses in clinical image review?

choices.rationale: Sharpness is one of the eight: margins of normal structures should be distinct.
Noise is one of the eight: it must not obscure or mimic structures.
Exam identification (labeling) is the eighth attribute.
Correct. Dose is controlled through equipment QC and the phantom dose limit, not scored as a clinical image attribute.

questions.explanation: The eight attributes are positioning, compression, exposure level, contrast, sharpness, noise, artifacts, and examination identification.

variants.simpler: The reviewers judge what they can see on the image. Dose isn't visible on the image, so it's not on the list.
variants.example: An overexposed image fails 'exposure level', but that's a judgment about visibility of structures, not a dose measurement.

questions.stem: An MQSA inspector asks how your facility reviews sample clinical images from each technologist and each interpreting physician. This question comes from which program?

choices.text: EQUIP (Enhancing Quality Using the Inspection Program)
choices.rationale: Correct. EQUIP's first inspection question covers facility procedures for ongoing clinical image quality, including regular sample-image review per technologist and interpreting physician.
The audit follows positive mammograms and correlates pathology; it isn't a sample-image quality review.
The physicist survey evaluates equipment and the facility's QC program, not technologist-by-technologist clinical images.
Complaint handling responds to consumers; it isn't a routine image review procedure.

questions.explanation: EQUIP added three inspection questions: ongoing clinical image quality review, corrective action for poor images, and lead interpreting physician oversight of QA/QC records.

variants.simpler: EQUIP is about the facility checking its own image quality between accreditation reviews.
variants.example: A log showing quarterly sample-image reviews for each technologist, with feedback notes, is EQUIP evidence.

questions.stem: How often must an accreditation body review clinical images from each facility it accredits?

choices.text: Every year, at the MQSA inspection
choices.rationale: Annual inspections are separate from accreditation clinical image review.
Two years isn't the stated frequency.
Correct. § 900.4(c)(1) sets review at least once every 3 years.

choices.text: Only when a complaint is received
choices.rationale: Additional reviews can follow concerns, but routine review is at least every 3 years.

questions.explanation: Clinical image review occurs at least once every 3 years. For each unit, CC and MLO views from two examinations are submitted and reviewed independently by two or more review physicians.

variants.simpler: Inspection: every year. Accreditation image review: every 3 years.
variants.example: A facility accredited in 2025 should expect its next clinical image review no later than 2028.

questions.stem: How many contact hours of documented mammography training does MQSA require for a technologist's initial qualification?

choices.rationale: 8 hours is the minimum training for each mammography modality, not the total initial training.
15 is the continuing education total required over 36 months.
25 is the number of exams performed under direct supervision.
Correct. At least 40 contact hours under a qualified instructor.

questions.explanation: Initial training is at least 40 contact hours, including anatomy and physiology, positioning and compression, QA/QC, and imaging patients with implants; plus 25 supervised exams and 8 hours per modality.

variants.simpler: 40 hours of training, 25 supervised exams, 8 hours per modality.
variants.example: A weekend course listing 16 contact hours covers less than half of the initial requirement.

questions.stem: A trainee is completing her 25 supervised mammograms. During one exam, her qualified supervisor is at the front desk but can be paged within a minute. Does this exam count toward the 25?

choices.text: Yes, because the supervisor is in the building and immediately available
choices.rationale: Being available isn't enough. Direct supervision requires the supervisor to be present to observe and correct.

choices.text: No, because direct supervision requires the supervisor to be present to observe and correct as needed
choices.rationale: Correct. This matches the § 900.2(o)(2) definition of direct supervision.

choices.text: Yes, if the supervisor reviews and signs the images afterward
choices.rationale: After-the-fact image review describes physician joint interpretation, not supervision of an exam.

choices.text: No, because only an interpreting physician can supervise exams
choices.rationale: Supervision is by an individual qualified as a technologist under § 900.12(a)(2).

questions.explanation: For an exam, direct supervision means the supervisor is present to observe and correct the person performing it.

variants.simpler: Supervisor in the room, watching: counts. Supervisor down the hall: doesn't.
variants.example: Documenting the supervisor's name for each training exam helps show the supervision was direct.

questions.stem: A newly qualified technologist trained only on FFDM. Her facility adds DBT next month. What does MQSA require before she performs DBT exams independently?

choices.text: At least 8 hours of continuing education in DBT
choices.rationale: Correct. Before using a modality not covered in initial training, the technologist needs at least 8 hours of CEUs in that modality.

choices.text: Another 40 contact hours of initial training
choices.rationale: The 40 hours are a one-time initial requirement; a new modality requires 8 hours.
25 supervised exams is the initial requirement and the experience-requalification path, not the new-modality rule.

choices.text: Nothing, if the facility's physicist approves the unit
choices.rationale: Equipment evaluation is separate from personnel training requirements.

questions.explanation: Each modality requires modality-specific training. For a modality added later, the rule is at least 8 hours of CEUs in it before independent use.

variants.simpler: New modality? Eight hours of training in it first.
variants.example: Vendor applications training can count if it's documented and meets the definition of a contact hour.

questions.stem: Which credential satisfies MQSA's general requirement for a radiologic technologist?

choices.text: A bachelor's degree in a physical science
choices.rationale: A physical-science degree relates to medical physicist qualifications, not technologists.
That is part of the mammography-specific requirement, not the general requirement.

choices.text: A State license for general radiography, or general certification from an FDA-recognized body
choices.rationale: Correct. Either satisfies § 900.12(a)(2)(i).

choices.text: A CPR certificate and facility orientation
choices.rationale: These may be employer requirements but are not MQSA's general requirement.

questions.explanation: The general requirement is State licensure for general radiography or general certification from an FDA-recognized body. Mammography-specific training is added on top.

variants.simpler: First you must be a qualified radiographer (license or certification). Mammography training comes after.
variants.example: A technologist certified in radiography by an FDA-recognized body meets the general requirement even in a State without licensure.

questions.stem: What is the MQSA continuing education requirement for radiologic technologists?

choices.text: 15 CEUs in mammography in 36 months, with at least 6 related to each modality used
choices.rationale: Correct. This matches § 900.12(a)(2)(iii).

choices.text: 24 CEUs in 24 months, any radiology topic
choices.rationale: ARRT biennial CE is a different program; MQSA counts mammography CEUs over 36 months.

choices.text: 15 category I CME credits in 36 months
choices.rationale: Category I CME is the interpreting physician requirement.

choices.text: 8 CEUs per year in each modality
choices.rationale: 8 hours is the new-modality minimum, not an annual requirement.

questions.explanation: 15 mammography CEUs in 36 months, at least 6 per modality used. A course taught several times counts once.

variants.simpler: Every 3 years: 15 hours of mammography CE, including 6 for each type of mammography you do.
variants.example: A technologist using FFDM and DBT needs at least 6 CEUs related to each, within the 15 total.

questions.stem: At inspection, a technologist has performed 170 mammograms in the facility's chosen 24-month window. What must happen before she resumes unsupervised mammography?

choices.text: She performs 30 more exams on her own to reach 200.
choices.rationale: Requalification requires supervised exams; performing unsupervised exams is what she can't do yet.
That's the CE requalification path; her shortfall is in experience.

choices.text: She performs at least 25 exams under direct supervision of a qualified technologist.

choices.rationale: Initial training isn't repeated for an experience shortfall.

questions.explanation: Continuing experience is 200 exams in 24 months. Falling short requires at least 25 exams under direct supervision of a qualified technologist before unsupervised work.

variants.simpler: Short on exam count? 25 supervised exams, then back to normal.
variants.example: A technologist returning from extended leave often faces exactly this situation.

questions.stem: A technologist performs FFDM and DBT. In the 36-month window she has 16 mammography CEUs: 12 related to FFDM and 4 related to DBT (each unit relates to one modality). What is the minimum additional CE she needs?

choices.text: None; she has more than 15 CEUs.
choices.rationale: The total is met, but DBT is below the 6-per-modality minimum.
Correct. Total 16 ≥ 15; FFDM 12 ≥ 6; DBT 4 needs 2 more to reach 6.
She already has 4 DBT CEUs; only 2 more are needed to reach 6.
The shortfall is modality-specific, so the additional units must relate to DBT.

questions.explanation: Check the total (15) and each modality (6) separately. Here only the DBT subtotal is short, by 2.

variants.simpler: Two checks: at least 15 total, and at least 6 for each modality. She passes the first, fails the second by 2.
variants.example: If she had 13 total (9 FFDM, 4 DBT), the same 2 DBT CEUs would fix both checks at once.

questions.stem: A facility's annual MQSA inspection is on August 20. Which end date may the facility choose for counting a technologist's 24-month exam total?

choices.text: Any date from June 30 through August 20
choices.rationale: Correct. The window may end on the inspection date, the last day of the preceding calendar quarter (June 30), or any date in between.
The facility has a choice; the inspection date is one option.
The calendar year end isn't one of the options.
The window is anchored to the inspection, not to employment dates.

questions.explanation: The facility picks the inspection date, the last day of the previous calendar quarter, or any date between. For an August 20 inspection, the preceding quarter ended June 30.

variants.simpler: Pick an end date between the end of last quarter and inspection day.
variants.example: For a February 5 inspection, the earliest choice is December 31.

questions.stem: Who has general responsibility for ensuring a facility's quality assurance program meets all MQSA requirements?

choices.rationale: The QC technologist handles tasks not assigned to the lead interpreting physician or medical physicist, but doesn't hold general responsibility.
The physicist performs surveys and equipment evaluations and oversees equipment-related QA.
MQSA assigns QA program responsibility to the lead interpreting physician; administrative titles are left to the facility.

questions.explanation: The lead interpreting physician has general responsibility for the QA program. Other individuals keep QA tasks only if the lead interpreting physician judges their qualifications and performance adequate.

variants.simpler: The lead physician is the captain of the QA team.
variants.example: Under EQUIP, inspectors ask how the lead interpreting physician oversees QC records.

questions.stem: The detector on Room 2's unit is replaced by service on Tuesday afternoon. What must happen before Room 2 is used for patient exams?

choices.text: The technologist runs the daily QC tests and resumes scanning if they pass.
choices.rationale: Major component replacement triggers a physicist's equipment evaluation; routine QC alone isn't sufficient.

choices.text: A mammography equipment evaluation by (or under direct supervision of) a medical physicist, with problems corrected first
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(e)(10) requires this after major components are changed or repaired.

choices.text: The accreditation body reviews new clinical images from the unit.
choices.rationale: Accreditation procedures may apply for new units, but the regulation's pre-use requirement here is the equipment evaluation.

choices.text: Nothing until the next annual survey
choices.rationale: Waiting for the annual survey would allow use of equipment not yet shown to meet standards.

questions.explanation: Installation, disassembly and reassembly, or major component change or repair requires a mammography equipment evaluation; all problems are corrected before clinical use.

variants.simpler: Big repair? The physicist checks it before patients.
variants.example: Converting a unit to add DBT makes it a new unit for MQSA purposes, which also requires evaluation before clinical use.

questions.stem: How long must QC records for a required test be kept?

choices.rationale: The rule isn't a fixed period.

choices.text: Until the next annual inspection is completed and FDA finds compliance, or until the test is performed two more times, whichever is longer

choices.rationale: Five years is a minimum retention for original mammograms and reports, not QC records.
Three years applies to serious complaint records.

questions.explanation: QC records are kept until the next annual inspection is completed with compliance found, or until the test has been done two additional times at its required frequency, whichever is longer.

variants.simpler: Keep QC records through the next clean inspection, and at least until the test has been done twice more.
variants.example: An annual test's record would usually be kept roughly two years, because two more annual performances take longer than reaching the next inspection.

questions.stem: Under MQSA, which final assessments define a 'positive mammogram'?

choices.rationale: Probably Benign isn't part of the positive definition.

choices.text: Incomplete: Need additional imaging evaluation and Suspicious
choices.rationale: Incomplete-additional imaging defines a screening recall, not a positive mammogram.

choices.text: Suspicious and Highly Suggestive of Malignancy
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.2(mm).

choices.text: Highly Suggestive of Malignancy and Known Biopsy-Proven Malignancy
choices.rationale: Known Biopsy-Proven Malignancy is reserved for known cancers; it isn't in the positive definition.

questions.explanation: A positive mammogram is assessed Suspicious or Highly Suggestive of Malignancy. That definition drives the PPV calculation and the 7-day reporting rule.

variants.simpler: Positive = Suspicious or Highly Suggestive.
variants.example: A Probably Benign result leads to follow-up, but it doesn't count as positive for PPV.

questions.stem: A report dated March 3 is assessed 'Incomplete: Need prior mammograms for comparison.' The outside facility hasn't sent the priors. What does the regulation require?

choices.text: Wait for the priors before issuing a final assessment, however long it takes.
choices.rationale: The follow-up report is due within 30 days whether or not comparisons are obtained.

choices.text: Issue a follow-up report with a final assessment within 30 calendar days of the initial report.
Convert the result to 'Probably Benign' automatically after 7 days.
choices.rationale: No automatic conversion exists; an interpreting physician issues the follow-up assessment.

choices.text: Repeat the exam to create new comparison images.
choices.rationale: Repeating the exam isn't the regulatory requirement and adds dose.

questions.explanation: If 'Incomplete: Need prior mammograms for comparison' is used, a follow-up report with a final assessment category must be issued within 30 calendar days of the initial report, whether or not comparison views can be obtained.

variants.simpler: Waiting for old films has a 30-day limit.
variants.example: From a March 3 report, the follow-up is due by April 2.

questions.stem: Which item must appear in the facility location on a mammography report but is NOT required in the facility location on the image label?

choices.rationale: City is required in both.
ZIP code is required in both.
Correct. The report's location includes the facility telephone number; the image label's location requires city, State, and ZIP code.
State is required in both.

questions.explanation: Report: city, State, ZIP, and telephone number. Image label: city, State, and ZIP code.

variants.simpler: The report needs a phone number so patients and providers can call; the image doesn't.
variants.example: A report template missing the facility phone number would need updating.

questions.stem: After a stereotactic biopsy, a mammogram is taken only to confirm the position of the tissue marker. Which MQSA assessment category is reserved for this?

choices.rationale: Benign describes benign findings on an interpreted mammogram; it isn't the marker-placement category.
This is reserved for known cancers being evaluated for definitive therapy.
Used when more imaging is needed before a final assessment.

questions.explanation: 'Post-Procedure Mammogram for Marker Placement' is reserved for a mammogram used to confirm deployment and position of a breast tissue marker.

variants.simpler: Clip check after biopsy has its own category.
variants.example: This category tells the reader the exam's purpose was the marker, not a new screening evaluation.

questions.stem: A screening mammogram is assessed Negative. Within what time must the patient receive the lay summary?

choices.rationale: The 7-day rule applies to Suspicious or Highly Suggestive results, counted from final interpretation.
15 days is the deadline for transferring records on request.
Every patient receives a lay summary within 30 days.

questions.explanation: Every patient receives a lay-language summary within 30 calendar days of the exam. It must include a breast density statement.

variants.simpler: Routine results: within 30 days.
variants.example: An exam on May 1 with a Negative result means the lay summary must reach the patient by May 31.

questions.stem: A diagnostic exam is performed on a Monday and the final interpretation on Thursday is 'Highly Suggestive of Malignancy.' The patient has a referring provider. Which timeline applies?

choices.text: Lay summary and provider report within 7 calendar days of Thursday
choices.rationale: Correct. For Suspicious or Highly Suggestive results, both are due within 7 calendar days of the final interpretation.

choices.text: Lay summary within 7 days of Monday; provider report within 30 days
choices.rationale: The 7-day clock runs from final interpretation, and the provider also gets the 7-day rule.
30 days applies to other results.

choices.text: Provider report within 7 days; the patient hears only from the provider
choices.rationale: The facility must still send the patient a lay summary.

questions.explanation: Suspicious and Highly Suggestive results trigger 7-calendar-day deadlines from the final interpretation for both the patient's lay summary and the provider's report.

variants.simpler: Worrying result: patient and provider both hear within 7 days of the final read.
variants.example: If the provider is unavailable, the report may go to a responsible designee within the same 7 days.

questions.stem: A self-referred patient names no healthcare provider. Her screening result is Probably Benign. What does MQSA require of the facility?

choices.text: Send only the lay summary; the full report goes to whichever provider she sees later.
choices.rationale: Patients without a named provider also receive the full report.

choices.text: Send the lay summary and the full report within 30 days, and use the facility's referral system to connect her with a provider
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(c)(2)(i)–(ii); Probably Benign is listed as a reason referral is clinically indicated.

choices.text: Decline to report until she names a provider.
choices.rationale: Facilities that accept self-referred patients must still provide results.

choices.text: Send the full report within 7 days.
choices.rationale: The 7-day rule is for Suspicious or Highly Suggestive results.

questions.explanation: A self-referred patient receives both the lay summary and the full report, and the facility's referral system applies when clinically indicated, including Probably Benign, Suspicious, or Highly Suggestive.

variants.simpler: No doctor named? She gets the full report too, and the facility helps her find a provider.
variants.example: A facility might keep a list of local clinics accepting new patients for this referral system.

questions.stem: For a Benign result, what is the latest the written report may reach the referring provider?

choices.text: As soon as possible, but no later than 30 days from the exam

choices.rationale: 7-day timelines apply to Suspicious or Highly Suggestive results.

choices.text: Within 15 days of the provider's request
choices.rationale: 15 days applies to transfer of records on request.
The limit is 30 days.

questions.explanation: Reports go to the referring or named provider as soon as possible and no later than 30 days. Failure to send within 30 days is listed as an adverse event.

variants.simpler: Provider report: 30 days at the latest.
variants.example: A batch of reports stuck in an interface queue past 30 days would be an adverse event to correct.

questions.stem: A report states 'The breasts are heterogeneously dense, which may obscure small masses.' Which statement must the patient's lay summary include?

choices.rationale: That statement goes with almost entirely fatty or scattered fibroglandular density.

choices.text: 'Your breast tissue is dense,' with the note that other imaging tests may help some people with dense tissue
choices.rationale: Correct. Heterogeneously and extremely dense map to the dense paragraph, § 900.12(c)(2)(iv).
'High/low density' was earlier wording; the current rule uses dense/not dense.

choices.text: No density statement; density is only for the provider.
choices.rationale: Since September 10, 2024, every lay summary includes a density statement.

questions.explanation: Four report categories map to two patient statements: the first two to 'not dense', heterogeneously and extremely dense to 'dense', with the added sentence about other imaging tests.

variants.simpler: The two denser categories → 'dense'. The two less dense → 'not dense'.
variants.example: Scattered areas of fibroglandular density → 'Your breast tissue is not dense.'

questions.stem: Where on the image must view and laterality be placed?

choices.rationale: The regulation specifies near the axilla.
Correct. § 900.12(c)(5)(iii).
Not obscuring anatomy is required for all labels, but view and laterality specifically go near the axilla.
The information must be indicated on the image.

questions.explanation: View and laterality are placed near the axilla, using standardized codes, and like all labels must not obscure anatomy.

variants.simpler: Side and view marker: by the armpit.
variants.example: On an RMLO, the 'RMLO' marker sits toward the axillary region of the image.

questions.stem: A facility has one mammography unit. Which label item is NOT required on its images?

choices.rationale: Always required.
Always required with the patient name.
Correct. Unit identification is required only if the facility has more than one unit.
Always required.

questions.explanation: Unit ID is conditional on having more than one unit. The other six items always apply.

variants.simpler: With only one machine, there's no doubt which one took the image.
variants.example: When a second unit is installed, unit identification becomes required on images from both.

questions.stem: A patient had one mammogram at a facility in 2021 and has not returned. The State has no longer requirement. Until at least when must the facility keep the original images and report?

choices.rationale: Five years applies when additional mammograms are performed at the facility.
Seven years isn't one of the MQSA periods.
Correct. With no additional mammograms at the facility, the minimum is 10 years.
MQSA sets minimums; indefinite retention isn't required.

questions.explanation: Retention is the longest of 5 years, 10 years if no additional mammograms at the facility, or State/local law.

variants.simpler: She never came back, so keep it 10 years.
variants.example: If State law required 12 years, the facility would keep it until 2033.

questions.stem: A patient asks your facility to send her DBT exam to another hospital for a second interpretation. Which response meets MQSA?

choices.text: Send printed key slices within 30 days.
choices.rationale: Printed slices aren't the original digital images, and the deadline is 15 days.

choices.text: Provide the original digital images electronically within 15 calendar days of the request.
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(c)(4)(ii)–(iii).

choices.text: Send a scanned copy of the report only.
choices.rationale: For final interpretation, the recipient needs the original digital images.

choices.text: Require the patient to pay a flat fee set by the facility, then send within 15 days.
choices.rationale: Fees may not exceed documented costs; a flat fee unrelated to cost isn't allowed.

questions.explanation: Transfers and copies occur within 15 calendar days. For digital mammography or DBT used for final interpretation, original digital images must be available electronically. Fees can't exceed documented costs.

variants.simpler: 15 days, original digital images, fair cost.
variants.example: Pushing the exam to the other hospital's PACS, or providing it on media in original DICOM format, preserves original digital images.

questions.stem: In the MQSA medical outcomes audit, the recall rate is the percentage of:

choices.rationale: Suspicious assessments feed PPV; recall rate uses screening exams assessed Incomplete-additional imaging.

choices.text: Screening mammograms assessed 'Incomplete: Need additional imaging evaluation'
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(f)(1)(iii).

choices.text: Patients who return for their next annual screening
choices.rationale: Return adherence isn't the audit's recall rate.

choices.text: Diagnostic mammograms that lead to biopsy
choices.rationale: Recall rate is defined on screening exams.

questions.explanation: Recall rate = screening mammograms assessed Incomplete: Need additional imaging evaluation ÷ screening mammograms.

variants.simpler: How often screening exams get called back for more pictures.
variants.example: 120 call-backs from 1,500 screens is a recall rate of 8%.

questions.stem: In a year, 2,500 patients were screened. Among them, 12 were diagnosed with breast cancer within 1 year after an Incomplete-additional imaging, Suspicious, or Highly Suggestive assessment. What is the cancer detection rate?

choices.rationale: This divides 12 by 25,000; the denominator is 2,500 patients.
The audit expresses cancer detection per 1,000 patients, and 4.8% would be 48 per 1,000.
This multiplies by 10,000 instead of 1,000.

questions.explanation: Cancer detection rate = qualifying cancers ÷ screened patients × 1,000. 12 ÷ 2,500 × 1,000 = 4.8 per 1,000.

variants.simpler: Divide cancers by patients screened, then multiply by 1,000.
variants.example: Same math: 9 cancers among 3,000 screened = 3 per 1,000.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old arrives for her routine annual mammogram but tells you she found a new lump last week. For audit purposes, how should this exam be classified?

choices.text: Screening, because it's her scheduled annual exam
choices.rationale: Scheduling doesn't decide it; a symptomatic patient's exam is diagnostic under the audit definition.

choices.text: Diagnostic, because she has a breast symptom
choices.rationale: Correct. Diagnostic exams are individualized views for patients with symptoms, physical signs, or abnormal screening findings.

choices.text: Screening, unless she asks for diagnostic
choices.rationale: Patient preference doesn't change the regulatory definition.

choices.text: Neither; it's excluded from the audit
choices.rationale: The audit covers all mammographic examinations.

questions.explanation: Screening = routine views of an asymptomatic patient. A new lump is a symptom, which makes the exam diagnostic for audit purposes. Follow your facility's protocol for routing it to a diagnostic work-up.

variants.simpler: Any symptom means diagnostic.
variants.example: Document the lump location on the history form so the interpreting physician knows the exam's purpose.

questions.stem: How long must a facility keep the record of each serious consumer complaint?

choices.rationale: Too short; the requirement is at least 3 years.
Five years is the minimum for original mammograms and reports.
The record is kept at least 3 years regardless of resolution.

questions.explanation: Serious complaint records are kept at least 3 years from receipt. Unresolved serious complaints are reported to the accreditation body.

variants.simpler: Serious complaint records: 3 years.
variants.example: A serious complaint received March 2026 stays on file until at least March 2029.

questions.stem: Which practice reflects the MQSA requirement for patients with breast implants?

choices.text: Ask about implants only if the order mentions them.
choices.rationale: Facilities must have a procedure to ask every patient before the exam.

choices.text: Ask before the exam and, unless contraindicated or modified by a physician, use views that maximize visualization of breast tissue
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(g).

choices.text: Perform only standard CC and MLO views to limit pressure on the implant.
choices.rationale: The regulation calls for views maximizing tissue visualization unless contraindicated.

choices.text: Refer all implant patients to MRI instead of mammography.
choices.rationale: MQSA doesn't require MRI referral; it requires an implant inquiry and appropriate views.

questions.explanation: Facilities need a procedure to ask about implants before the exam, and use views that maximize visualization of breast tissue unless contraindicated or modified by a physician.

variants.simpler: Always ask about implants first, then image to see as much tissue as safely possible.
variants.example: A patient may not mention implants unless asked, especially years after surgery.

questions.stem: What is the MQSA limit on average glandular dose for a single CC view of an FDA-accepted phantom simulating a standard breast?

choices.rationale: Not the regulatory limit.
Correct. § 900.12(e)(5)(vi); the same maximum applies to other modalities under (e)(6).
The limit is per exposure, for a single CC view of the phantom.
Ten times too high.

questions.explanation: 3.0 mGy (0.3 rad) per exposure for a single CC view of a phantom simulating a standard breast (4.2 cm, 50/50), with clinical technique. It is a phantom test limit, not an individual patient's measured dose.

variants.simpler: The test phantom can't receive more than 3 mGy per picture.
variants.example: If the physicist measures 3.4 mGy for the phantom CC view, the dose test fails and must be corrected before further exams.

questions.stem: On a digital unit, the morning phantom image fails the manufacturer's action limits. What does MQSA require?

choices.text: Continue scanning and correct the problem within 30 days.
choices.rationale: Other-modality QC failures are in the group that must be corrected before further exams.

choices.text: Identify the problem and correct it before performing further exams on that unit
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(e)(8)(ii)(A) includes (e)(6), the QC program for non-screen-film modalities.

choices.text: Repeat the test once; if it passes, ignore the failure.
choices.rationale: A failure requires identifying the source and taking corrective action, not ignoring it.

choices.text: Wait for the physicist's annual survey.
choices.rationale: Waiting would allow exams on a failing system.

questions.explanation: Digital (other-modality) QC failures must be corrected before further exams. Only tests outside the listed group allow 30 days.

variants.simpler: Failing phantom on digital: fix it before the next patient.
variants.example: Patients scheduled on that unit may be moved to another unit that passed QC.

questions.stem: Which statement about the compression device meets MQSA equipment requirements?

choices.text: Initial compression may be hand-cranked from one side only.
choices.rationale: Initial compression is power-driven with hands-free controls operable from both sides.

choices.text: A flat paddle may deflect from parallel by up to 2.0 cm.
choices.rationale: The limit is 1.0 cm.

choices.text: The chest-wall edge of the paddle must be straight, parallel to the receptor edge, and must not appear on the image.
Spot paddles must be the same size as the full-field receptor.
choices.rationale: Special-purpose paddles, including spot paddles smaller than the receptor, are permitted.

questions.explanation: Power-driven, hands-free initial compression and fine adjustment from both sides; flat paddles deflect no more than 1.0 cm; the chest-wall edge is straight and parallel and must not appear on the image.

variants.simpler: Motorized from both sides, nearly flat, and the edge shouldn't show on the image.
variants.example: A visible paddle-edge line along the chest wall of a clinical image would point to a paddle problem.

questions.stem: How often is a certified mammography facility inspected by a certified MQSA inspector?

choices.rationale: Correct. FDA's MQSA program page cites 42 U.S.C. 263b(g)(1)(E).

choices.text: Every 3 years with clinical image review
choices.rationale: Three years is the accreditation body's image review cycle.
Inspections are routine; complaints can lead to additional review.
Inspections continue at least annually.

questions.explanation: Facilities are inspected at least annually. Separately, accreditation bodies review clinical images at least every 3 years.

variants.simpler: Inspection: yearly.
variants.example: CE and experience windows are anchored to this annual inspection date.

questions.stem: How many examinations under direct supervision are part of a technologist's initial MQSA mammography requirements?

choices.rationale: 8 hours is the per-modality training minimum.
15 is the continuing education total over 36 months.
200 is the continuing experience requirement over 24 months.

questions.explanation: Initial mammography requirements include at least 25 examinations under direct supervision.

variants.simpler: 25 supervised exams to start.
variants.example: The same number, 25, is the requalification path for an experience shortfall.

questions.stem: At inspection, a technologist has 11 mammography CEUs in the 36-month window. What is required before she resumes unsupervised mammography?

choices.text: Obtain enough CEUs to total at least 15 in the previous 3 years, with at least 6 per modality used
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(a)(2)(iii)(D).
That's the experience requalification path.

choices.text: Nothing; CE shortfalls are noted but not enforced
choices.rationale: She may not perform unsupervised exams until CE is complete.
Only enough CEUs to reach the requirement are needed.

questions.explanation: A CE shortfall is fixed by bringing the total to at least 15 in the prior 3 years, with at least 6 per modality, before resuming unsupervised exams.

variants.simpler: Short on CE: make it up before working alone.
variants.example: With 11 CEUs she needs at least 4 more, and must still meet 6 per modality.

questions.stem: Which MQSA assessment category is reserved for a known cancer being imaged before definitive therapy?

choices.rationale: Used for findings with a high probability of malignancy, not already proven cancer.
Used for findings with a definite probability of malignancy.
Used when more imaging is needed before a final assessment.

questions.explanation: 'Known Biopsy-Proven Malignancy' is reserved for known malignancies being evaluated for definitive therapy.

variants.simpler: Already-diagnosed cancer has its own category.
variants.example: A pre-surgical exam to map extent of a biopsy-proven cancer uses this category.

questions.stem: A report states 'There are scattered areas of fibroglandular density.' The patient's lay summary must say:

choices.rationale: Correct. Scattered fibroglandular density maps to the not-dense paragraph, § 900.12(c)(2)(iii).
That statement is for heterogeneously or extremely dense.
Earlier wording; replaced by dense/not dense.
Every lay summary includes a density statement.

questions.explanation: Almost entirely fatty and scattered fibroglandular density both map to 'Your breast tissue is not dense.'

variants.simpler: Scattered = not dense.
variants.example: The same paragraph still tells the patient to talk with her provider about density and risk.

questions.stem: Which item is required on every mammographic image under MQSA?

choices.rationale: The interpreting physician is named in the report, not on the image.
An additional patient identifier is required, but the regulation doesn't specify date of birth.
Technique display is an equipment requirement, not an image label item.

questions.explanation: Image labels include technologist identification along with patient name and additional identifier, date, view and laterality, facility name and location, cassette/screen ID, and unit ID when there's more than one unit.

variants.simpler: The image shows who took it; the report shows who read it.
variants.example: Technologist initials or ID code on each image let QA reviews give individual feedback.

questions.stem: Within how many calendar days must a facility transfer original mammograms after the patient requests it?

choices.rationale: 7 days applies to Suspicious or Highly Suggestive results.
Not an MQSA timeline.
30 days applies to reports and lay summaries.

questions.explanation: Transfers and copies are completed within 15 calendar days of receiving the request.

variants.simpler: Records request: 15 days.
variants.example: A request received June 1 must be fulfilled by June 16.

questions.stem: A facility issued 40 positive mammograms in its audit period. Within 1 year, 10 of those patients were diagnosed with breast cancer. What is the PPV?

choices.rationale: This inverts the ratio (40 ÷ 10 = 4) and reads it as a percentage.
This uses the cancer count as the percentage.
This uses the positive-mammogram count as the percentage.

questions.explanation: PPV = patients with positive mammograms diagnosed with cancer within 1 year ÷ patients with positive mammograms × 100%.

variants.simpler: Of the 40 called positive, 10 were cancer: one in four.
variants.example: If 12 of 40 were cancer, PPV would be 30%.

questions.stem: A referring physician calls to complain that a patient's mammography report never arrived. Under MQSA, who counts as a 'consumer' who may complain?

choices.rationale: Consumers include representatives of the patient.

choices.text: The patient or a representative such as a family member or the referring provider
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.2(k).
Staff concerns are handled internally; consumers are patients and their representatives.
The accreditation body receives unresolved serious complaints; it isn't the consumer.

questions.explanation: A consumer is anyone who comments or complains about an exam: the patient or a representative such as a family member or referring provider. A missing report is also a possible adverse event.

variants.simpler: Patients, families, and their doctors can all complain.
variants.example: The facility's written complaint system should capture complaints from all three.

questions.stem: A clinic proposes adding a mammography attachment to its general-purpose radiographic unit. Under MQSA, this unit:

choices.text: May be used if the physicist approves the attachment
choices.rationale: The prohibition applies regardless of physicist evaluation.

choices.text: May be used for screening only
choices.rationale: The prohibition isn't limited by exam type.

choices.text: May not be used for mammography
choices.rationale: Correct. § 900.12(b)(1) prohibits general-purpose equipment, including modified systems with special attachments.

choices.text: May be used if dose stays below 3.0 mGy
choices.rationale: Meeting the dose limit doesn't override the equipment prohibition.

questions.explanation: Radiographic equipment designed for general purpose or special non-mammography procedures, including systems modified with mammography attachments, may not be used for mammography.

variants.simpler: Only machines built for mammography can do mammography.
variants.example: A mammography unit, at minimum, includes its own generator, control, tube housing, beam-limiting device, and supporting structures.
